title: Meier et al. (2016) True/False Quiz
instructions: Choose True or False. Check article-level denominators, overlapping stakeholder categories, and the scope of conclusions. The frequency with which a theme appears in studies is not an individual preference score or a universal ranking of what matters at the end of life.

items.prompt: The included qualitative and quantitative studies had roughly comparable sample sizes, so sample-size differences were negligible.
items.explanation: Reported sample sizes ranged from 3 to 2,548, and qualitative studies generally had much smaller samples than quantitative studies. The review therefore combined studies with markedly different sample sizes.

items.prompt: The concept of a good death arose from the hospice movement and has been described as a multifaceted, individualized experience.
items.explanation: The introduction traces the concept to hospice and discusses the importance of the dying person's perspective. It also notes criticism of imposing a single external criterion for a good death.

items.prompt: The authors reported no overlapping participant samples among the studies included in the review.
items.explanation: After removing duplicate articles and checking relevant reference lists, the authors reported no overlapping samples. This is separate from an article containing more than one stakeholder perspective.

items.prompt: All 3,042 records excluded at title-and-abstract screening were duplicate versions of the same articles.
items.explanation: Most initial exclusions reflected irrelevant topics, such as cell, bone, or animal death. Duplicate articles were removed separately; irrelevance and duplication were different exclusion reasons.

items.prompt: The reported geographic distribution included seven studies from Japan and three from the United Kingdom.
items.explanation: The review reported seven studies from the United Kingdom and three each from Japan and the Netherlands. These are counts of included studies, not population estimates of end-of-life preferences.

items.prompt: The authors described the distribution of men and women across the reviewed studies as relatively even overall.
items.explanation: This is the authors' summary across studies. It does not mean that every individual study included equal numbers of men and women.

items.prompt: The life-completion theme included saying goodbye, feeling that life had been well lived, and accepting impending death.
items.explanation: The researchers grouped these three subthemes under life completion. They represent concerns identified in the literature, not requirements that every dying person must meet.

items.prompt: When the two coders disagreed, one coder's judgment was accepted automatically and a third author was never involved.
items.explanation: The coders discussed discrepancies and consulted a third author when needed to reach a final consensus. Disagreement resolution was part of the coding process.

items.prompt: Relationships with healthcare providers were identified as a distinct core theme, separate from treatment preferences.
items.explanation: This theme included trust, support, and comfort from clinicians, their comfort with dying, and discussion of spiritual beliefs or fears. Its frequency in articles does not determine how important that relationship is to an individual patient.

items.prompt: Patients did not view emotional well-being as part of a good death; this theme appeared only in family and healthcare-provider perspectives.
items.explanation: The review interprets emotional well-being as an important component in patients' perspectives as well as those of families and healthcare providers. It calls for attention to psychological concerns alongside physical symptoms.

items.prompt: Each of the 36 articles was assigned exclusively to one stakeholder category, so the patient, family, and healthcare-provider article counts must sum to 36.
items.explanation: Seven articles included more than one stakeholder perspective. The counts of 20 patient-perspective, 10 family-perspective, and 18 healthcare-provider articles therefore overlap and should not be added as mutually exclusive groups.

items.prompt: Religiosity or spirituality appeared in a greater proportion of patient-perspective articles (65%) than family-perspective articles (50%).
items.explanation: Table 3 reports this theme in 13 of 20 patient-perspective articles and 5 of 10 family-perspective articles. These are article-level frequencies, not percentages of individual patients or family members and not proof of a statistically significant difference in personal priorities.

items.prompt: The included studies consistently reported the interval between interviews or surveys and patients' deaths, allowing adjustment for changes in preferences as death approached.
items.explanation: The review identifies the lack of reported timing as a limitation. Wishes, needs, and understandings of a good death may change as death approaches, so that missing information matters for interpretation.

items.prompt: The authors suggest that differences in hospice use and the lack of on-site clergy or spiritual counselors in some settings may have influenced recognition of religious or spiritual concerns.
items.explanation: Not all patients received hospice services, and the authors discuss limited availability of spiritual-care staff, especially for diverse patient groups. This is a possible contextual explanation, not a tested effect or a claim that every patient wants religious care.

items.prompt: The authors propose future mixed-methods studies comparing people near the end of life with people at earlier stages of chronic illness and including different age cohorts.
items.explanation: The proposed research would examine how illness stage and age relate to definitions of a good death and develop standardized, validated measures. These are future directions, not comparisons or treatment effects established by this review.
